description: Team NyeoClipse is a solo AI engineering entry tackling MODIS and VIIRS thermal hotspot harmonization. Using deep learning, statistical sensor fusion, and vector-space architecture, we bridge the gap between legacy 1km MODIS and modern 375m VIIRS satellite telemetry to build unified wildfire and climate timelines.
summary:
Elipsis is a web application that turns NASA satellite fire detections into an accessible map, burning-activity calendar, and historical investigation workspace. It addresses the MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge by helping users explore where and when burning activity was reported and compare observations from satellites with different detection characteristics.

Our current archive contains more than 56 million reported detections across India, the United States, Canada, Brazil, and Australia. Users can select locations and dates, inspect satellite records, explore seasonal patterns, and export their findings with source provenance.

For evaluated Indian regions, Elipsis also compares MODIS and VIIRS activity using a common spatial grid and eight-day periods, with regional adjustments referenced to Aqua. Original observations remain accessible, and unsupported comparisons are clearly identified.

Elipsis makes complex Earth-observation records easier for students, researchers, and environmental analysts to investigate responsibly. Its central principle is transparency: a satellite hotspot is a reported detection, not automatically a separate fire, and missing observations must never be mistaken for an absence of burning.
details:
Elipsis is a browser-based workspace for investigating historical burning activity using genuine NASA FIRMS observations. It combines a geographic explorer, activity calendar, historical review, cross-satellite comparison, and downloadable evidence in one interface.

The current release contains 56,768,918 retained detections from 97 annual country files. It covers India from 2011–2025 and the United States, Canada, Brazil, and Australia from 2021–2025, respecting each satellite product’s actual availability. A separate Punjab pilot and earlier evaluation artifacts are preserved for reproducibility.

How it works

The processing pipeline acquires official NASA historical CSV files, retains the originals, records source URLs and SHA-256 checksums, and converts observations into partitioned Parquet datasets for efficient local querying. Satellite identity, acquisition time, confidence, fire radiative power, and literal product versions remain traceable.

Users select a country, dates, satellite, and quality filters. India additionally supports state-level and custom-area investigation. The workspace displays matching observations, temporal patterns, and source attributes. CSV exports and companion provenance use the applied selection and dataset revision, helping ensure that exported evidence matches the displayed analysis.

How we address the challenge

MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions, sensitivities, and observation times. Directly comparing their raw hotspot totals can therefore produce misleading conclusions.

Elipsis's evaluated harmonization workflow summarizes activity as occupied 5 km equal-area grid cell-days within non-overlapping eight-day UTC windows, separating daytime and nighttime observations. It fits empirical scaling factors against MODIS Aqua to express eligible VIIRS activity in Aqua-equivalent units.

The preserved India transfer study used 2018–2021 for training, 2022 for validation, and 2023–2024 for evaluation. It tested All India, Punjab state, western Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh. These results measure agreement with Aqua, which is a comparison reference rather than ground truth. Earlier exposure to Punjab evaluation data is documented, and calibration is not automatically transferred to the newly added countries.

Benefits and intended impact

Elipsis helps students, researchers, and environmental analysts investigate seasonal burning, compare historical periods, and examine whether apparent changes depend on sensor selection or analytical choices. Downloadable records and self-contained offline briefs support further investigation and communication.

Additional tools examine candidate cross-satellite correspondences, sensitivity to methodological choices, thermal-source context, and comparable periods. Workflows requiring weather, ground validation, burn-scar polygons, or other external evidence explicitly request those inputs rather than inventing results.

Creativity and design considerations

The project connects a visual burning-activity calendar with transparent comparison methods and an evidence trail. Users can move from an apparent pattern to its underlying observations, assumptions, and exports.

We considered usability, accessible navigation, reproducibility, performance, differing sensor confidence systems, boundary provenance, and incomplete satellite observation coverage. Zero reported detections, unavailable records, and unknown observation coverage remain distinct. Hotspot counts are never presented as unique fire incidents or burned hectares.
